text: If you set your own exam, studied those very questions, and then graded yourself, a perfect score would tell nobody anything about what you know. Judging a model on the data it learned from is the same mistake. The fix is simple to say and surprisingly easy to get wrong: keep some data aside that the model never learns from, and use it only for judging.

The usual arrangement cuts the data into three parts. The training set is the textbook: the model fits its weights to it. The validation set is the mock exam: we use it to make choices the training cannot make for itself, such as the degree of a polynomial or the strength of regularisation. The test set is the final exam, sealed in an envelope and opened once, at the very end, to give an honest estimate of how the finished model will do on new data.

Why not use the test set for those choices as well? Because every time you pick the option with the best score, a little information about that data leaks into your decisions. Try fifty settings and keep the winner, and part of its score is luck that happened to suit those particular examples. If that luck came from the test set, the test score is now optimistic, and the sealed envelope has quietly become just another mock exam.

How you cut matters too. Data often arrives in some order, sorted by date or grouped by label, and slicing off the last part would give the test set a different kind of example from the training set. So we shuffle first, with a fixed random seed so the split can be repeated. Time is the exception: when predicting the future, train on the past and test on later data, because shuffling would let the model peek at tomorrow.

When data is scarce, setting a large validation set aside hurts. Cross-validation shares the burden. Split the training data into, say, five folds; train on four and validate on the fifth, then rotate until every fold has served once as the validation set, and average the scores. Every example gets used for both learning and judging, just never in the same round.

One subtle leak catches experienced people. Preprocessing has parameters too: if you standardise features using the mean and spread of the whole dataset before splitting, the test set has already shaped your training data. Compute those statistics on the training set alone, then apply the very same numbers to validation and test, as if the test data arrived tomorrow.

Language models face this problem at enormous scale. Because they are trained on huge scrapes of the web, the questions of a public benchmark can end up in the training text, which researchers call contamination, and a model may then appear to reason when it is partly remembering. Next, we meet a method that does no training at all, k nearest neighbours.
